newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's Tung wins early approval for property stance.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung wins early approval for property stance.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa won a favourable reaction to his partially revealed long-term property policy, but analysts say he appears to have little to combat another surge in this overheated real estate market.
"His comments were better than expected. There will be no fiscal measures, no punitive measures," said Alan Siu, lecturer at the School of Economics and Finance at Hong Kong University.
"He is absolutely correct in saying there is no scarcity of land and to promise to increase the number of residential housing units put on the market."
Tung, a former shipping tycoon who was handpicked by Beijing to run the territory, took over as chief executive after Hong Kong reverted to Chinese rule on Tuesday.

At a news conference on Wednesday, his second day as chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Tung reaffirmed he would take supply side action to curb the upward spiral of residential property prices.
His chief tool would be to increase the number of residential units brought to the market each year to 85,000 for the next 10 years.

"This is the right policy, the right way of going about things," said Peter Perkins, regional strategist at Daiwa Institute of Research. "Prices have moved dramatically out of line with people's incomes."
Tung reiterated his policy would not include restrictive, punitive measures such as those taken to curb speculation in 1994. He also ruled out slapping additional taxes on homebuyers.

"We are relieved he is not taking drastic short-term measures," said Amy Wong, research director at New China Hong Kong Securities. "This is a long-term problem which needs serious, long-term attention."
The stock market had feared harsh immediate action which would cap or erode the 30 percent rise in residential property prices seen so far in 1997, analysts said.
As yet, Tung did not appear to have a short-term anti-speculation programme.
"Tung doesn't want to implement austerity measures unless property prices surge to unreasonable levels," said investment analyst Manfred Ho at ING Barings.
The new government's long-term aim would be to increase home ownership to 70 percent, Tung said. Estimates state 50-56 percent of Hong Kong households own their own home.
At the moment, there are 150,000 people on a seven-year waiting list to buy homes, Tung said on Wednesday.
But analysts said the parts of the plan Tung has revealed showed little difference from the British colonial government's long-term housing programme released in January.
"Only there will be more emphasis on public housing," said Ho.

From 1997-2001, Tung will stick to the pre-handover government plan, under which not less than 85,000 units would be brought to market each year -- 54,000 units public housing units and 31,000 units from private sector developers, Ho said.
But Tung's plan would provide 85,000 units per year from 2002-2006, instead of the 73,000 units the former administration had proposed, he said.
In the past 15-20 years, Hong Kong's Housing Authority has built an average of 25,000 residential units per year.
"Private housing supply will not be too great and should not kill the market," Ho added.
Ho believes that under Tung's plan Hong Kong's property developers would continue to see a moderate uptrend in prices.
And Tung's comments contained a very interesting, positive sign, Siu said.
"Tung hinted he would sell off public housing flats," said Siu. "I think if this is implemented, this is a very important thing."
"Essentially public tenants do not have the vehicle to share the prosperity of Hong Kong of the past 20 years. Now if you give them the property cheap, they can share in the prosperity," Siu said.
"This will make the wealth distribution in Hong Kong a bit more even, a win-win situation for everybody."
